classification.difficultyReason: Applies odd and even vertex degrees to construct a route and justify why a closed route is impossible.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 12, shared figure above parts (a) and (b)
spec.description: Upright square with both diagonals and a triangular roof. Five filled vertices; the diagonal crossing is unmarked. Source grey edges are rendered black under house style. Coordinates describe visual proportions, not numerical givens.
spec.mathematics: Eight edges. The two lower vertices have degree 3, the two upper square vertices have degree 4, and the apex has degree 2. The diagonal crossing is not a vertex.
spec.answerVisibility: Complete supplied figure remains visible; no route or solution labels are printed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Can you draw the figure without lifting your pen, travelling along each edge exactly once? Vertices may be revisited.

answer.short: Yes. Begin at either lower corner and finish at the other.
answer.worked:
One route is: lower left → upper left → apex → upper right → upper left → lower right → upper right → lower left → lower right.

This uses each of the eight edges exactly once. The two lower corners each have three incident edges, so they are the start and finish. At every other vertex, entering and leaving pair the edges.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that it is not possible to draw the figure if you are required to begin and end at the same point.

answer.short:
Impossible.

A closed route pairs entering and leaving edges at every vertex, but each lower corner has three edges.
answer.worked:
If the route begins and ends at the same point, every arrival at a vertex is paired with a departure, including at the starting vertex. Each vertex must therefore have an even number of incident edges.

Both lower corners have three incident edges. Since three is odd, the figure cannot be drawn along each edge exactly once in a closed route.
